ledger.sentence: An X-ray uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation to make an image of the inside of the body.
ledger.note: North Cumbria leaflet: X-ray imaging uses a beam of electromagnetic radiation.

ledger.sentence: According to the NHS, X-rays can produce images of many parts of the body, including bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system.
ledger.note: NHS: X-rays image bones, teeth, lungs and the digestive system.

ledger.sentence: They are used, for example, to check for broken bones after an accident.
ledger.note: NHS: used to detect problems such as bone fractures.

ledger.sentence: The health professional who takes X-rays in hospital is called a radiographer.
ledger.note: NHS: radiographers are the trained staff who take the images.

ledger.sentence: The radiographer positions the person sitting, lying or standing, depending on the part of the body.
ledger.note: Newcastle trust: staff may ask you to sit, lie down or stand depending on the part examined; NHS says the radiographer may ask you to move into different positions.

ledger.sentence: The X-ray itself takes only a few minutes, according to the NHS.
ledger.note: NHS: the X-ray itself should only take a few minutes.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says people are asked to remove metal items such as jewellery and zips.
ledger.note: NHS: avoid wearing jewellery and clothes containing metal such as zips, as these will need to be removed.

ledger.sentence: Some types need fasting for several hours beforehand.
ledger.note: A trust says for some specific examinations people are told in advance to avoid eating and drinking for a few hours.

ledger.sentence: The NHS lists several related tests, including angiography, which checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood.
ledger.note: NHS: angiography checks blood vessels using a dye injected into the blood.

ledger.sentence: It also lists DEXA scans, which measure bone density, and CT scans, which give more detailed images.
ledger.note: NHS: DEXA measures bone strength; CT gives more detailed images.

ledger.sentence: Studies of the digestive system use a barium drink or enema, a liquid that shows up on X-ray.
ledger.note: NHS: barium swallow involves drinking barium; barium enema puts barium into the bowel via the rectum.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small.
ledger.note: NHS page retrieved says the cancer risk is thought to be very small and a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects; words 'safe' and 'serious complications are rare' not found.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says the risk of cancer from X-rays is thought to be very small.
ledger.note: NHS: cancer risk thought to be very small; link to 'lots of X-rays' not found in retrieved NHS text.

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets say staff keep doses as low as possible and that a test goes ahead only when its benefit outweighs the small risk.
ledger.note: Worcestershire: doses kept as low as reasonably practicable; Cornwall and Bath leaflets: benefit should outweigh the risk.

ledger.sentence: GOV.UK safety advice says that when imaging is properly justified and optimised, the risks from X-ray examinations are far smaller than the risks of the conditions being investigated.
ledger.note: GOV.UK: when properly justified and optimised, risks are much less than the risks of the conditions being investigated.

ledger.sentence: GOV.UK safety advice says cancers linked to radiation can take decades to appear.
ledger.note: GOV.UK retrieved: cancers take decades to appear, especially relevant for older patients; 'very small' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The same advice says children have a higher lifetime risk from X-rays than adults, and that risk is lower for older patients because cancers take a long time to develop.
ledger.note: GOV.UK: children have an increased lifetime risk depending on age and sex; risks lower for older patients since cancers take decades.

ledger.sentence: Trusts ask anyone who might be pregnant to tell the team before an X-ray.
ledger.note: Retrieved: most leaflets ask people to tell staff if they might be pregnant.

ledger.sentence: NHS trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage and, at typical doses, do not cause birth defects.
ledger.note: Retrieved: NHS leaflets say X-rays in pregnancy do not raise miscarriage risk and do not cause birth defects at typical doses; Leicester attribution not exact.

ledger.sentence: The main concern it names is a very small increase in the chance that the baby develops cancer in childhood.
ledger.note: Retrieved: main concern is a very small increase in childhood cancer risk (Leicester).

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets say X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care during pregnancy.
ledger.note: Retrieved: tummy X-rays need special care; 'usually avoided' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: A trust leaflet says X-rays of parts of the body away from the tummy, such as the head, chest, arms or lower legs, are fine to have during pregnancy.
ledger.note: Retrieved: a trust leaflet says X-rays away from the tummy, such as head, chest, arms or lower legs, are OK. Dental not confirmed; 'do not give any increased risk' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: A test may go ahead during pregnancy if the health benefit clearly outweighs the small radiation risk to the baby.
ledger.note: Retrieved: a test may go ahead in pregnancy if the health benefit clearly outweighs the small risk to the baby.

ledger.sentence: A reporting radiographer or a radiologist, a doctor who specialises in imaging, reviews the X-ray.
ledger.note: NHS: images go to a radiologist or specially trained radiographer who reports.

ledger.sentence: The report goes to the team that requested the test.
ledger.note: Reports go back to the referring clinician.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says results may come on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later, and that a clinician should explain them.
ledger.note: NHS: results may be the same day or at an appointment a few weeks after; a healthcare professional should explain them.

ledger.sentence: Trusts quote different waits for the report, so timings differ between hospitals.
ledger.note: Trust pages quote different waits (about ten working days to two weeks); urgency link not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: An X-ray can produce images of many parts of the body, and the NHS lists fractures, teeth, lungs and the digestive system among them.
ledger.note: As claims 2 and 3.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says a standard X-ray leaves no after-effects and the cancer risk is thought to be very small.
ledger.note: As claims 14 and 15: 'safe' and 'serious complications rare' not confirmed in retrieved NHS text.

ledger.sentence: Trust leaflets say X-rays during pregnancy do not raise the risk of miscarriage, and that X-rays of the tummy or near the womb need special care.
ledger.note: Retrieved: no miscarriage increase and no birth defects at typical doses; tummy X-rays need special care. 'Usually avoided' not retrieved.

ledger.sentence: The NHS says results may be given on the same day or at an appointment a few weeks later.
ledger.note: NHS says results may be the same day or at an appointment a few weeks after; dependence on type of X-ray not retrieved.
